title: Holly Candidates
text:
Purpose
American holly (Ilex opaca) is evergreen, so in leaf-off imagery (flown February to March 2025) its crowns stay green while the deciduous canopy around it is bare. This page builds the first step of a holly classification workflow:

Candidates from imagery (this page): find small, isolated evergreen crowns in non-developed areas.
Ground truth: visit candidate locations and record what is there (holly, sex if known, or the false-positive species).
Classification: train a supervised classifier on crown features (and NDVI once the 4-band imagery arrives) using the field labels, then map holly across the transect.









Step
Script
Output




7. Crown extraction
R/06_holly_objects.R
data/derived/holly_objects.gpkg (all crowns with features)


8. Candidate rule
holly_candidates() in R/functions.R
data/derived/holly_candidates.{csv,gpx} (field list)



The current imagery is RGB only, so greenness comes from the green leaf index (GLI). When the 4-band imagery arrives and the mosaic is rebuilt with a nir band, veg_index() switches to NDVI automatically; only the NDVI thresholds in config.yml need calibrating.

title: Holly Candidates
text:
Why NDVI
Healthy leaves treat red and near-infrared (NIR) light very differently. Chlorophyll absorbs most red light for photosynthesis, while the internal cell structure of a leaf (the spongy mesophyll) scatters and reflects most NIR light. Bare branches, dead or dormant grass, soil, and pavement show much less of this contrast. The normalized difference vegetation index captures it in one number:
\[
\text{NDVI} = \frac{\text{NIR} - \text{Red}}{\text{NIR} + \text{Red}}
\]
NDVI ranges from −1 to 1. Water is negative, soil, rock, and pavement sit near 0, and dense green foliage is typically above 0.6. Because it is a ratio, it is also less sensitive to illumination than a single band, so a shaded crown and a sunlit crown of the same tree give similar values.
This contrast is what makes leaf-off imagery useful for holly. In February and March the deciduous canopy is bare and has low NDVI, while evergreen foliage stays green and has high NDVI. Holly in the understory should stand out clearly against the bare hardwoods around it.
The RGB stand-in used here, the green leaf index (GLI), relies only on the small green reflectance peak of leaves in visible light. In this imagery GLI separates pine canopy (median about 0.03) from leaf-off hardwood (about −0.02) by only a narrow margin. It is also affected by shadows and by the imagery’s slight blue cast. That narrow margin is why the current candidates include many false positives.

Measuring the gain from NIR
When the 4-band imagery arrives, the same crowns will be described with both indices. Once field labels exist, the comparison will use the same ground-truth set and the same spatially blocked cross-validation for two classifiers:

Visible only: crown features from RGB (GLI, colour, brightness, size, shape, isolation).
Visible + NIR: the same features plus NDVI and NIR reflectance.

The improvement will be reported as the change in precision (share of candidates that are holly), recall (share of holly found), and overall accuracy, along with how many candidates drop out of the field list.

title: Holly Candidates
text:
Approach
Each 12-inch tile is processed at full resolution:

Vegetation index (GLI (green leaf index, RGB)), smoothed with a 3 × 3 px mean.
Crowns: pixels with index > 0.05 are evergreen crown; connected groups of them are crown objects. Objects 6–30 ft across (equivalent-circle diameter) are kept with their features.
Isolation: the share of evergreen pixels (index > 0.02, a lower threshold) in the 70 ft neighbourhood of each crown. Holly in a leaf-off hardwood stand has a low share; a crown inside pine canopy has a high one.
Candidate rule: crown 10–20 ft across, evergreen share ≤ 0.25, and NLCD class not water or developed (11, 21, 22, 23, 24). Crowns cut by a tile edge are excluded from the field list.

Thresholds were set by inspecting forest chips at 17.5 and 22.5 km: GLI in pine canopy has a median near 0.03, leaf-off hardwood near −0.02.

Example
A 600 × 600 ft area 22.5 km along the transect: a pine stand (upper left) next to leaf-off hardwoods (lower right). Candidates are the isolated crowns in the hardwood stand; crowns inside the pine canopy are rejected as not isolated.


Code
ends <- st_coordinates(line)[, 1:2]
d <- (ends[2, ] - ends[1, ]) / sqrt(sum((ends[2, ] - ends[1, ])^2))
p <- ends[1, ] + km_to_crs(22.5) * d
e <- ext(p[1] - 300, p[1] + 300, p[2] - 300, p[2] + 300)
chip <- crop(load_ortho(aoi = FALSE), e)
names(chip) <- band_names(chip)
vi <- focal(veg_index(chip, vi_name), h$smooth_px, "mean", na.policy = "omit")
ex <- obj[st_as_sf(as.polygons(e, crs = crs(chip))), ]
ex <- ex[ex$reason %in% c("candidate", "not isolated"), ]

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5))
plotRGB(chip, mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5)); title("Imagery with crowns")
plot(vect(ex), add = TRUE, border = reason_cols[ex$reason], lwd = 2)
legend("bottomleft", c("candidate", "not isolated"), col = reason_cols[c("candidate", "not isolated")],
       lwd = 2, bg = "white", cex = 0.8)
plot(vi, main = vi_label, axes = FALSE, legend = TRUE, mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 4),
     col = hcl.colors(50, "Greens 3", rev = TRUE))

Along the transect
Candidate density per km² of non-developed land (NLCD classes other than 11, 21, 22, 23, 24) in each 1 km window, with the window’s forest cover for reference.


Code
nondev <- classes |>
  filter(!class %in% h$exclude_nlcd) |>
  group_by(window) |>
  summarise(nondev_frac = sum(frac))
dens <- windows |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  left_join(nondev, by = "window") |>
  left_join(count(st_drop_geometry(cand), window, name = "n"), by = "window") |>
  left_join(select(nlcd, window, forest_pct), by = "window") |>
  mutate(n = coalesce(n, 0L),
         nondev_km2 = area_km2 * nondev_frac,
         per_km2 = ifelse(nondev_km2 > 0.05, n / nondev_km2, NA))

plot_ly(dens, x = ~u_mid_km) |>
  add_bars(y = ~per_km2, name = "Candidates per km² non-developed",
           marker = list(color = "#d95f02"),
           customdata = ~sprintf("%d candidates in %.2f km²", n, nondev_km2),
           hovertemplate = "%{y:.0f} per km² (%{customdata})<extra></extra>") |>
  layout(xaxis = list(title = "Distance from Richmond (km)", dtick = 5),
         yaxis = list(title = "Candidates per km²"),
         hovermode = "x unified", showlegend = FALSE) |>
  config(displaylogo = FALSE)








Candidate gallery
A random sample of candidates, 60 × 60 ft around each crown (outlined), for a quick visual check of what the rule picks up.


Code
set.seed(2025)
ortho <- load_ortho(aoi = FALSE)
samp <- cand[sample(nrow(cand), min(24, nrow(cand))), ]
par(mfrow = c(4, 6), mar = c(0.2, 0.2, 1.2, 0.2))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(samp))) {
  ctr <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(st_geometry(samp[i, ])))
  x <- crop(ortho, ext(ctr[1] - 30, ctr[1] + 30, ctr[2] - 30, ctr[2] + 30))
  plotRGB(x[[1:3]], mar = c(0.2, 0.2, 1.2, 0.2))
  plot(vect(samp[i, ]), add = TRUE, border = "#d95f02", lwd = 1.5)
  where <- if (is.na(samp$window[i])) "end cap" else sprintf("window %d", samp$window[i])
  title(sprintf("%.0f ft, %s", samp$diam_ft[i], where), cex.main = 0.8, line = 0.2)
}

Features recorded for every crown, compared between candidates and crowns rejected as not isolated (mostly crowns within pine or other evergreen canopy). These are the starting inputs for the classifier.

title: Holly Candidates
text:
Ground truth
The field list is data/derived/holly_candidates.csv (with a GPX copy for GPS units and phone apps). Each row has the crown id, latitude and longitude, transect position, crown diameter, and the features used by the rule. Suggested field record per visited candidate:







Field
Values




obj_id
crown id from the list (or new id for holly found nearby but not listed)


species
Ilex opaca, or the false positive (e.g. eastern red cedar, pine, magnolia, privet, ivy-covered trunk, lawn)


sex
female (fruit), male, unknown


dbh_cm, height_m
optional size measures


notes, photo
free text and photo id



Crown ids are tied to the current thresholds; if the rule or index changes, match field records to crowns by location rather than id. Keep field data outside data/derived/ (for example data/field/), since derived files are rebuilt by the scripts.

title: Holly Candidates
text:
Next steps

Sampling design: a stratified random sample of candidates per window (or per NLCD class), so the field effort covers the full gradient.
Classifier: with field labels, fit a supervised model (e.g. random forest) on crown features, validated with spatially blocked cross-validation (hold out whole windows).
NDVI: when the 4-band imagery arrives, rebuild the mosaic, calibrate the NDVI thresholds, and add NDVI and NIR features. In leaf-off imagery NDVI should separate evergreen foliage from bare branches and dormant grass more cleanly than GLI.

title: Holly Candidates
text:
Notes

Expected false positives: other evergreens of similar size, such as eastern red cedar, young loblolly or Virginia pine, southern magnolia, and evergreen shrubs (privet, Elaeagnus, mountain laurel), plus green ground cover such as winter grass or English ivy on trunks.
What is missed: holly under evergreen canopy (hidden), crowns smaller than 10 ft, holly in developed areas (excluded by design), and crowns merged with neighbouring evergreens into one larger object.
Shadows: the imagery has long shadows in places; shaded crowns may fall below the index threshold.

title: Study Area and Orthoimagery
text:
Notes

Imagery source: VBMP 2025 12-inch orthoimagery (Sanborn Map Company, flown February to March 2025), distributed by the Virginia Geographic Information Network (VGIN). The MrSID versions are RGB only. The near-infrared band is only in the TIFF deliverables.
Tile layout: each 12-inch tile is 5,000 × 5,000 px at 1 ft, covering 5,000 × 5,000 ft. Tile names follow DO_S13_<section>_<quarter>.2025.
MrSID decoding: the MrSID GDAL driver only loads inside the QGIS application (macOS code-signing blocks it from the command line), so conversion runs in the QGIS Python console.
Mosaic edges: the VRT has no nodata value. Areas outside the tiles read as 0 in all three bands; all such areas lie outside the study area.

title: Licensed to Ilex
text: This site documents spatial analyses components of this project using the 2025 Virginia Base Mapping Program (VBMP) 12-inch orthoimagery along a 25 km transect from industrial Richmond, Virginia (37.584817° N, 77.472433° W) to Pocahontas State Park (37.373768° N, 77.570813° W), buffered by 2 km on each side. The overall goal here is to identify smampling zones, target trees, and establish a set of individuals along the gradient to serve as focal trees along a mulitfaceted gradient from highly developed Richmond Virginia \(\to\) Pochontas State Park.

title: Licensed to Ilex
text:
Analyses




Analysis
Description




01
Study area and orthoimagery
Transect, study area, imagery tiles, and mosaic


02
Urban to forest gradient
Annual NLCD land cover and impervious surface in 1 km windows along the transect


03
Holly candidates
Small, isolated evergreen crowns in leaf-off imagery as candidate holly locations for ground truth

title: Licensed to Ilex
text:
Framing

Urbanization is treated as a continuous gradient, not an urban-versus-rural comparison. The goal is to identify “phase shifts” from urban to peri-urban to secondary forest, with applied value for managing human-modified landscapes.
It builds directly on the dogwood work: about 60 maternal trees sampled from Richmond to Pocahontas State Park, with mating system parameters analyzed against spatial, impervious surface, and land cover gradients.
Holly is framed as an Anthropocene “winner,” like pigeons and rats, a species doing well in human landscapes that’s worth understanding for that reason.

title: Licensed to Ilex
text:
Questions

Sex ratios: Holly is dioecious, and the nursery trade sells grafted female clones. Urban areas may be female-biased, which could lower seed set through limited pollen.
Pollination: Little is known about who pollinates holly. The visitors appear to be mostly generalists. One hypothesis is that non-native urban pollinators compensate, so there’s no net effect on seed set.
Herbivory: The holly leaf miner and its parasitoids, including possible co-evolution along the gradient.
Leaf traits and physiology: Leaf toughness, LI-COR gas exchange, and water-use efficiency, linked to herbivore performance (modeled on the Costa Rica caterpillar study).
Fragmentation: Holly often grows on forest edges, so edge versus interior is a related axis.
Longer term: Reciprocal common gardens (Rice Rivers Center and an urban site near the Science Museum), and range-wide phylogeography, including high-elevation Appalachian populations.

title: Licensed to Ilex
text:
Approach

Start with low-cost observational data:

Map and sex trees after leaf drop,
Collect seeds from mother trees through December (freezer storage),
Photograph leaves on target trees for herbivory,
Rear leaf miners for parasitoids,
Run pollinator counts in April–June.
Germination tests, seed abortion, etc. ~ (landscape location).

title: Licensed to Ilex
text:
People

Recruit undergraduates by pitching to targeted courses: GIS/cartography for spatial work, ecology for herbivory & pollinators, and evolution for co-evolution.
Formats include independent study, the new zero-credit research course, and a possible fall capstone or seminar that produces the literature review.
An NSF submission is planned.

Code
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(leaflet)
library(terra)
library(here)

source(here("R", "functions.R"))
derived <- here(cfg$paths$derived)

line    <- load_transect()
aoi     <- load_aoi()
windows <- load_windows()
nlcd    <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "nlcd_windows.csv"))
classes <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "nlcd_window_classes.csv"))
lc      <- rast(here(cfg$nlcd$dir, sprintf("LndCov_%d.tif", cfg$nlcd$year)))

# Join on the window id only; the distance columns are floats and may not match exactly
windows <- left_join(windows, select(nlcd, -u_start_km, -u_end_km, -u_mid_km, -area_km2), by = "window")

# Grouped cover, ordered from most to least urban; colors follow the NLCD legend
cover_cols <- c(
  developed      = "#eb0000",
  developed_open = "#dec5c5",
  barren         = "#b3ac9f",
  agriculture    = "#dcd939",
  shrub_grass    = "#ccb879",
  forest         = "#38814e",
  wetland        = "#b8d9eb",
  water          = "#466b9f"
)
cover_labels <- c(
  developed = "Developed (low to high)", developed_open = "Developed, open space",
  barren = "Barren", agriculture = "Agriculture", shrub_grass = "Shrub and grassland",
  forest = "Forest", wetland = "Wetland", water = "Water"
)

title: Urban to Forest Gradient
text:
Purpose
A first look at how land use changes from downtown Richmond to Pocahontas State Park. The study area is cut into non-overlapping 1 km windows along the transect, each spanning the full 4 km buffer width, and each window is summarized from the Annual NLCD 2025 land cover and fractional impervious surface layers (30 m).

NLCD is kept on its native grid (EPSG:5070). Windows are projected to it and summarized with exactextractr, which weights each 30 m cell by the fraction of it inside the window.

The charts below are interactive: hover to read every value at one distance, click a legend entry to hide it (double-click to show it alone), and drag to zoom (double-click to reset). Lines connect window midpoints, so values between midpoints are interpolated.


Code
library(plotly)

# Shared x axis and landmarks
river_km  <- nlcd$u_mid_km[which.max(nlcd$water_pct)]
end_km    <- max(nlcd$u_end_km)
x_axis <- list(title = "Distance from Richmond (km)", range = c(0, end_km),
               dtick = 5, zeroline = FALSE, showgrid = FALSE)
landmarks <- list(
  list(x = 0, y = 1.02, yref = "paper", text = "Richmond", showarrow = FALSE,
       xanchor = "left", yanchor = "bottom", font = list(size = 12)),
  list(x = end_km, y = 1.02, yref = "paper", text = "Pocahontas State Park", showarrow = FALSE,
       xanchor = "right", yanchor = "bottom", font = list(size = 12)),
  list(x = river_km, y = 1.02, yref = "paper", text = "James River", showarrow = FALSE,
       yanchor = "bottom", font = list(size = 12, color = "#466b9f"))
)
river_line <- list(type = "line", x0 = river_km, x1 = river_km, y0 = 0, y1 = 1,
                   yref = "paper", line = list(color = "#466b9f", width = 1, dash = "dot"))
plotly_cfg <- function(p) {
  config(p, displaylogo = FALSE,
         modeBarButtonsToRemove = c("lasso2d", "select2d", "autoScale2d"))
}



Land cover composition
Share of each window in each grouped cover type. Developed land is stacked from the bottom and forest above it, so the urban-to-forest transition reads as the green band widening toward Pocahontas State Park.


Code
p <- plot_ly()
for (k in names(cover_cols)) {
  p <- add_trace(p, data = nlcd, x = ~u_mid_km, y = nlcd[[paste0(k, "_pct")]],
                 type = "scatter", mode = "lines", stackgroup = "cover",
                 name = cover_labels[[k]], fillcolor = cover_cols[[k]],
                 line = list(color = "white", width = 0.5),
                 hovertemplate = paste0(cover_labels[[k]], ": %{y:.1f}%<extra></extra>"))
}
p |>
  layout(xaxis = c(x_axis, list(hoverformat = ".1f")),
         yaxis = list(title = "Share of window (%)", range = c(0, 100), ticksuffix = "%"),
         hovermode = "x unified",
         legend = list(traceorder = "reversed"),
         annotations = landmarks, shapes = list(river_line),
         margin = list(t = 40)) |>
  plotly_cfg()








Impervious surface and forest
Mean fractional impervious surface and forest cover per window. The shaded band is ± 1 SD of impervious surface among the 30 m cells in each window, a measure of how mixed the window is.


Code
imp_col <- "#5e3c99"
for_col <- "#38814e"
band <- nlcd |> mutate(lo = pmax(imperv_mean - imperv_sd, 0), hi = pmin(imperv_mean + imperv_sd, 100))

plot_ly(band, x = ~u_mid_km) |>
  add_ribbons(ymin = ~lo, ymax = ~hi, name = "Impervious ± 1 SD",
              fillcolor = "rgba(94, 60, 153, 0.15)", line = list(width = 0),
              hovertemplate = "Impervious ± 1 SD: %{customdata}<extra></extra>",
              customdata = ~sprintf("%.0f–%.0f%%", lo, hi)) |>
  add_trace(y = ~imperv_mean, type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers", name = "Impervious surface",
            line = list(color = imp_col, width = 2), marker = list(color = imp_col, size = 8),
            hovertemplate = "Impervious surface: %{y:.1f}%<extra></extra>") |>
  add_trace(y = ~forest_pct, type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers", name = "Forest",
            line = list(color = for_col, width = 2), marker = list(color = for_col, size = 8),
            hovertemplate = "Forest: %{y:.1f}%<extra></extra>") |>
  layout(xaxis = c(x_axis, list(hoverformat = ".1f")),
         yaxis = list(title = "Percent", range = c(0, 100), ticksuffix = "%"),
         hovermode = "x unified",
         legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.2),
         annotations = landmarks, shapes = list(river_line),
         margin = list(t = 40)) |>
  plotly_cfg()

title: Urban to Forest Gradient
text:
Notes

Data: Annual NLCD Collection 1, 2025 land cover (LndCov) and fractional impervious surface (FctImp), read for the AOI bounding box from the USGS web coverage service (https://dmsdata.cr.usgs.gov/geoserver). No resampling or reprojection of the rasters.
Developed combines NLCD classes 22–24 (low, medium, high intensity). Developed open space (21) is mostly lawns, parks, and road verges and is kept separate. Forest is classes 41–43; wetland is 90 and 95.
Windows are not replicated samples. Adjacent windows are spatially autocorrelated, so the curves describe the gradient but should not be treated as 25 independent observations.
The 4 km width averages across very different ground on either side of the line (e.g. the James River crossing near 5–7 km). A narrower center band would test how much that matters.
